title: How to Make Artificial Intelligence More Environmentally Sustainable
gist: Charles Humble (GOTO Copenhagen) argues AI's electricity and emissions growth makes sustainability a top-level architectural concern, citing Microsoft emissions +30% since 2020 and Google +50% since 2019. He prescribes pre-built/smaller models, carbon-aware demand shifting and shaping, and green-grid siting, noting inference over a model's lifetime may outweigh training emissions.

themes.theme: AI-driven hyperscaler power and emissions growth

insights.claim: According to the IEA, combined electricity use of Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta more than doubled between 2017 and 2021, reaching around 72 TWh in 2021.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler power demand was compounding even before the generative AI build-out.
insights.quote: the combined electricity use from Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta has more than doubled between 2017 and 2021, rising to around 72 terawatt-hours in 2021
insights.locator: Humble quoted the International Energy Agency

insights.claim: Microsoft's 2024 environmental report states its total carbon emissions rose 30% since 2020, primarily due to data center construction for AI demand.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: AI capex is directly eroding hyperscaler climate commitments.
insights.quote: Microsoft’s 2024 environmental report mentioned that its total carbon emissions have risen 30% since 2020, primarily due to the construction of data centers to meet demand for AI
insights.locator: Humble quoted the International Energy Agency

insights.claim: Google's self-reported emissions surged about 50% since 2019 and 13% year on year in 2023, largely driven by AI.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Embodied and operational AI emissions are now material line items in big-tech ESG reporting.
insights.quote: Google’s emissions had surged about 50% since 2019 and 13% year on year in 2023 alone
insights.locator: Humble quoted the International Energy Agency

insights.claim: The IEA estimated 2022 global data centre electricity use at 240-340 TWh (1-1.3% of global demand), with networks adding 260-360 TWh, for a total of roughly 700 TWh, comparable to Brazil's 726 TWh.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Data centres plus networks consume electricity on the scale of a large national economy.
insights.quote: That’s 700 terawatt hours, about the same as Brazil’s 726 terawatt hours in the same time period.
insights.locator: The IEA estimated that global data

insights.claim: IT is responsible for roughly 2-4% of global emissions versus about 3% for aviation, but unlike aviation, the IT industry is increasing rather than cutting its emissions.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Tech may face aviation-style regulatory and reputational scrutiny on emissions.
insights.quote: But while the aviation industry is working quite hard to try and cut its emissions, we as an industry are doing the opposite.

insights.claim: Warming is targeted at 1.5 degrees by 2100, but projections suggest roughly 2.5 to 3 degrees.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Context for tightening pressure on high-growth energy consumers like AI.
insights.quote: We want to keep our warming to 1.5 degrees by 2100, but projections suggest that it will be between about 2.5 and 3 degrees.

insights.claim: Humble argues sustainability should join cost, performance, security, regulatory concerns and reliability as a top-level consideration for computing workloads.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Carbon may become a first-class non-functional requirement alongside cost and SLA.
insights.quote: Sustainability ought to join cost, performance, security, regulatory concerns, and reliability as one of the top-level considerations for your computing workloads

insights.claim: Humble proposes a business-context checklist for AI: do you really need it, can you use a pre-built model instead of training from scratch, can a relaxed SLA allow greener locations, and can you use demand shaping.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Gating questions that reduce unnecessary AI compute demand.

insights.claim: Humble's four steps for greener computing: use the smallest hardware that safely runs the job, run in regions with abundant low-carbon electricity and credible decarbonisation plans, choose cloud providers with green-located data centres and footprint tooling, and optimize job execution time.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Cloud providers with clean-grid regions and carbon tooling gain a selection advantage.
insights.quote: Use the smallest hardware configuration that can safely execute the job.

themes.theme: Carbon-aware computing: demand shifting and shaping

insights.claim: A workload uses fixed energy, but its carbon cost varies enormously by location and time; running on grids dominated by hydro, solar, nuclear and wind such as Norway, Sweden and France can be many times cleaner than coal- or gas-dependent grids.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Low-carbon grids become a competitive siting advantage for data centres.
insights.quote: running a workload here can be many times cleaner than one dependent on coal or gas
insights.locator: Charles Humble: A compute workload uses

insights.claim: Demand shifting can be time-based or location-based; time-based shifting suits latency-insensitive work like AI training, while advanced location shifting could move workloads between hemispheres seasonally to follow solar power.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Training workloads are geographically and temporally mobile in ways inference is not.
insights.quote: More advanced variations might involve moving to different hemispheres seasonally to maximize exposure to sunlight and solar power.

insights.claim: Demand shaping changes how much or what kind of work software does based on grid cleanliness, e.g. letting users choose a human over the AI, serving lower-quality media, disabling autoplay, or using a smaller model during high carbon intensity, at the cost of added complexity.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Carbon-responsive graceful degradation is a new product design pattern.
insights.quote: Demand shaping means changing how much work your software does, or what kind of work, in response to how clean or constrained the electricity supply is at that moment.

insights.claim: Humble claims training on 100% renewable energy could in theory cut carbon emissions by between 45% and 99%.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Renewable PPAs are a large lever for training emissions specifically.
insights.quote: In theory, training can be on 100% renewable energy all the time, which can reduce carbon emissions somewhere between 45% and 99%

insights.claim: Humble argues most energy may be spent when models are deployed and maintained in production rather than in training; for widely used models, lifetime inference emissions may exceed training emissions.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Inference efficiency, not training, is the larger long-run energy problem.
insights.quote: Keep in mind that for widely used models, inference over the model’s lifetime may cause greater total emissions, so efficiency in serving matters too.

insights.claim: To green training, Humble advises avoiding training from scratch in favour of fine-tuning pre-trained models, prompting or RAG, and compressing models via distillation, quantization and pruning; federated on-device training can be greener in some cases.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Supports demand for smaller, compressed and pre-trained models over bespoke frontier training.
insights.quote: avoid training from scratch if at all possible

insights.claim: Humble argues smaller models sometimes work better and teams should question how much data they actually need to collect.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Bigger is not always better; small models can be both cheaper and greener.
